newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS-Russia, seeking cash, may tax domestic debt.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Russia, seeking cash, may tax domestic debt.

text.p: Russian officials, desperate to rake in extra cash to meet promises to the International Monetary Fund, agreed on Thursday to tax the lucrative domestic debt market next year.

But ministers and parliamentary deputies who make up a commission re-examining the government's 1997 budget draft revised down plans for overall tax revenue, vetoing higher taxes on petrol and keeping tax exemptions on some investment.
Economists said new taxes on securities might increase the government's borrowing costs.
"Yields will rise exactly by the volume of the tax," said an analyst at the Finance Ministry's economic expert group.

Low tax revenues are one of Russia's acutest economic problems -- the country received 74 percent of budgeted taxes in the first nine months of 1996 -- and the shortfall forced the IMF to delay payment of a tranche of its $10 billion loan to Russia earlier this month.

But Itar-Tass news agency quoted First Deputy Finance Minister Vladimir Petrov as saying that tax collection had improved in the second half of October, when the government collected 10.6 trillion roubles.
Tax revenue was three trillion roubles in the first half of the month, Petrov told a government meeting. He was sure Russia would get the next IMF tranche by the end of this year.
IMF officials have made clear they are looking for clear evidence that tax collection has improved and this improvement can be sustained before they decide to release the delayed cash.
The commission, including parliamentarians wary of current revenue forecasts, is trying to work out what to do next year.
Zadornov said Thursday's proposal would ask the State Duma lower house of parliament to impose new taxes on operations with government securities.
Such operations are currently tax-exempt and earlier this month the Duma rejected a planned 15 percent tax on government discount GKO Treasury bills.

Duma representatives suggested bringing back export duties on oil and gas and increasing average import tariffs to 15 percent from the current 13.7 percent -- ideas bound to annoy both the government and the IMF.

"The final decision of the export duties problem will depend on the calculations for replacing them which we shall receive tomorrow," said Mikhail Zadornov, head of the lower house's budget committee and a member of the conciliation commission.

The Duma rejected the government's first 1997 draft budget earlier this month, complaining about the revenue forecasts and inadequate provisions for Russia's growing army of poor. The commission was set up to try to hammer out a compromise.

Officials acknowledge that revenue plans are ambitious but say they will only accept higher spending if it is matched by higher taxes. Both the new and the original draft plan a budget deficit of 90.70 trillion roubles ($16.6 billion).
